context: Binary executes another program. If called with user-influenced arguments while elevated, could be used to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges.

References encryption method configuration, typically sourced from /etc/login.defs. A SUID binary reading or influencing encryption method selection could weaken system-wide password hashing if the method is manipulable or insufficiently strong.
References minimum password length configuration. If this binary reads or writes password policy, misconfiguration could weaken system authentication.
References maximum password length configuration. Some implementations truncate passwords silently, which can weaken security or indicate policy manipulation.
References the delay after a failed authentication attempt. If manipulable, an attacker could reduce or eliminate brute force delay.
Explicit reference to a fake or substitute shell. Presence in a SUID binary is highly suspicious and warrants immediate investigation.
References system group ID boundaries. A SUID binary reading or writing GID configuration could be used to manipulate group membership or escalate group privileges.
Binary can change file ownership. If called while elevated and the target path is user-influenced, could be used to take ownership of sensitive files.
Binary can change file permissions. If called while elevated and the target path is user-influenced, could be used to make sensitive files world-readable or executable.
Binary modifies terminal attributes. Can affect terminal input handling. If not restored properly, may leave the terminal in an insecure or broken state.
Binary spawns child processes. Combined with execve or shell references in the same binary, may indicate a pattern worth investigating for process injection or privilege inheritance.
Binary reads the current login name. If used for authentication or authorization decisions without proper validation, could be spoofed in some environments.
Binary attempted to drop elevated privileges and failed. If execution continues after this failure, the binary may be running with unintended elevated privileges.
Binary references the sudo password helper path. If this environment variable is read without sanitization, an attacker could point it to a malicious program to intercept sudo password prompts.
FUSE mount option that permits root to access a user-mounted filesystem. Combined with a permissive /etc/fuse.conf, could allow a malicious userspace filesystem to intercept root file access.
Binary spawns a shell. If privileges are not dropped before the shell is executed, the spawned shell may inherit elevated privileges.

Binary constructs a PATH dynamically with a variable component. If the variable is user-influenced, an attacker may be able to inject a malicious directory into the PATH and hijack binary execution. Associated with CVE-2021-4034 in pkexec.
Binary calls setuid() system call. If not properly managed, could retain elevated privileges after initialization or allow privilege escalation.
Binary calls setgid() system call. If not properly managed, could retain elevated group privileges after initialization.
Binary checks effective user ID. Indicates awareness of privilege state. Verify privilege dropping occurs after this check completes.
Binary checks effective group ID. Indicates awareness of privilege state. Verify privilege dropping occurs after this check completes.
Binary initializes supplementary group access. May indicate privilege dropping routine, but verify groups are reduced appropriately.
Binary changes root directory. If escape vectors exist in the jail, an attacker with elevated privileges could break out and access the full filesystem.
Binary changes the root mount point. Similar risks to chroot, but with additional complexity. Privilege escalation through improper isolation is a known attack vector.
Binary can trace/debug other processes. With elevated privileges, could inspect or modify memory of system processes, extract credentials, or bypass security controls.
Binary sets Linux capabilities. Misconfigured capability assignments could grant dangerous permissions without full root, enabling targeted privilege escalation.
Binary reads process capabilities. Indicates awareness of capability state. Verify capabilities are appropriately restricted.
Binary invokes prctl() for various process control operations. Some options can alter privilege behavior, memory protection, or debugging restrictions.
Binary allocates memory mapping. With MAP_SHARED or specific protections, could enable exploitation techniques like heap spraying or return-to-libc attacks.
Binary executes programs searching PATH. If PATH is influenced by untrusted input, could execute attacker-controlled binaries with elevated privileges.
Binary invokes shell command execution. Any unvalidated input passed here constitutes a command injection vulnerability when combined with SUID privileges.
Binary opens a pipe to a command processor. Similar risk to system(), allows command injection if arguments derive from untrusted sources.
Binary executes another program directly. Verify all arguments are validated; format string vulnerabilities in arguments could enable exploitation.
Binary executes with explicit environment. If environment variables are user-controllable, could set LD_PRELOAD or similar to hijack execution.
Binary references dynamic linker preload. SUID binaries must sanitize or ignore this environment variable, otherwise attackers can load malicious shared libraries with root privileges.
Binary references library search path. Similar risk to LD_PRELOAD - uncontrolled values can redirect library loading to attacker-provided code.
Binary reads HOME directory. If used to locate config files or scripts, user-controlled home paths could point to malicious resources.
Binary uses custom temporary directory. Unprivileged users may create symlinks or race conditions in controlled temp locations, enabling TOCTOU attacks.
Binary accesses passwd file. Write access enables account creation or privilege manipulation; read-only access is generally safe but indicates privilege checks.
Binary accesses shadow password file. Unauthorized read or write access compromises authentication security and enables credential theft or manipulation.
Binary modifies sudoers configuration. Enables persistent privilege escalation for any user. Extremely high-risk operation for a SUID binary.
Binary manages cron jobs. With elevated privileges, could schedule tasks that persist beyond session, creating backdoors or data exfiltration mechanisms.
Binary references password management. Legitimate use exists (e.g., /usr/bin/passwd), but verify it follows secure password-changing protocols.
Binary references sudo command. May indicate privilege escalation chaining or integration with sudo authentication mechanisms.
Binary references su command. May spawn subshells with privilege transitions. Verify input validation and session handling.
Binary performs filesystem mounting. Could mount privileged filesystems or bind-mount sensitive directories with elevated access.
Binary unmounts filesystems. Could deny service by unmounting critical mounts or disrupt system availability.
Binary creates special device nodes. With SUID privileges, could create character/block devices granting direct hardware or kernel interface access.
Binary creates hard links. Limited impact but could enable symlink race conditions or overwrite protected files if permissions allow.
Binary creates symbolic links. Similar risk to link() - could facilitate TOCTOU attacks on protected resources.
Binary deletes files. With elevated privileges, could remove security logs, configuration files, or evidence of compromise.
Binary renames files. Could disrupt security controls by moving configuration files or interfering with backup/archive systems.
Binary changes file ownership. Similar to fchown but operates by pathname, introducing symlink race vulnerabilities in the lookup phase.
Binary changes file permissions. Similar to fchmod but operates by pathname, introducing symlink race vulnerabilities in the lookup phase.
Binary looks up user by name. Part of normal privilege checking routines, but verify resulting UID/GID calculations are applied safely.
Binary looks up group by name. Part of normal privilege checking routines, but verify resulting group memberships are applied safely.
Binary sets supplementary group list. With elevated privileges, could add user to privileged groups (wheel, sudo, etc.) enabling persistent escalation.
Binary duplicates file descriptors. Could redirect input/output of privileged operations to attacker-controlled files or network sockets.
Binary creates network sockets. With elevated privileges, could establish covert channels, bypass firewall rules, or connect to privileged ports.
Binary initiates network connections. Could exfiltrate data, communicate with remote attacker C2, or abuse network-level access controls.
Binary binds to network ports. Could listen on privileged ports (<1024), impersonate legitimate services, or establish unauthorized daemons.
Binary listens for incoming connections. Combined with bind(), could create network services running with elevated privileges.
Binary accepts incoming connections. Could receive commands or data from remote sources with elevated privilege context.
Binary sends network data. Potential for data exfiltration or abuse of network privileges depending on destination.
Binary receives network data. Could ingest commands or payloads from untrusted sources.
Binary performs device I/O control. Device-specific commands may expose kernel interfaces, hardware controls, or memory access depending on target device.
Binary checks file accessibility. Use of access() is often unsafe due to TOCTOU races; verify realpath() or similar is used for actual operations.
Binary resolves canonical path. Positive sign indicating awareness of symlink attacks, but verify results are validated before use.
Binary retrieves file metadata. Part of normal file operations but verify results are validated before permission decisions.
Binary retrieves file metadata without following symlinks. Better than stat() for security-sensitive checks, but verify symlink targets are validated.
Binary reads symbolic link target. May indicate awareness of symlink attacks, but verify targets are validated before operations.
Binary reads current working directory. If used in path construction, relative paths could escape intended directories.
Binary changes working directory. If target is user-influenced, could escape sandboxed directories or operate on unexpected locations.
Binary locks files. Could deny service by holding locks on critical resources or create race conditions with improper lock release.
Binary sets alarm timer. Could interfere with timeout mechanisms or timing-dependent security controls.
Binary handles signals. Improper signal handlers could enable race conditions, signal injection, or privilege retention through handler bugs.
Binary sends signals to processes. With elevated privileges, could terminate critical services, crash system processes, or trigger privileged code paths.
Binary adjusts process priority. Could deny CPU resources to legitimate processes or prioritize malicious operations.
Binary reads process priority. Generally benign but indicates process management capabilities.
Binary sets process priority. Could affect system responsiveness or prioritize malicious processes.
Binary queries or sets resource limits. Could remove constraints on file descriptors, memory, or other resources enabling resource exhaustion attacks.
Binary reads or sets system hostname. If writable, could affect hostname-based access controls or audit logs.
Binary retrieves system information. Generally benign but could leak kernel version for exploit targeting.
Binary retrieves system hostname. Used for identification or access control decisions.
Binary retrieves real user ID. Standard privilege check, but verify effective UID is checked separately.
Binary retrieves real group ID. Standard privilege check, but verify effective GID is checked separately.
Binary retrieves parent process ID. Could be used to detect execution context (e.g., spawned from restricted shells).
Binary retrieves its own process ID. Standard operation, generally benign.
Binary waits for child process completion. Part of normal fork/exec patterns, verify child cleanup is thorough.
Binary waits for specific child process. Similar to wait() but allows more control over child reaping.
Binary terminates without cleanup. Could leave locked resources or incomplete operations if called prematurely.
Binary terminates abnormally. May dump core with sensitive memory contents if core dumps are enabled.
Binary registers exit handlers. Could clean up resources but also hide cleanup of malicious state.
Binary sets environment variables. With elevated privileges, could set dangerous variables (LD_PRELOAD, PATH) affecting subsequent executions.
Binary sets environment variables. Similar risk to putenv() - verify all environment modifications are intentional and safe.
Binary clears environment variables. Good security practice for stripping dangerous variables, verify all dangerous vars are cleared.
Binary clears entire environment. Strong security practice if followed by selective restoration of safe variables.
Binary generates random values. Verify source is cryptographically secure (/dev/urandom or getrandom()) not predictably seeded.
Binary uses rand() function. Typically predictably seeded; verify usage doesn't affect security-sensitive operations.
Binary seeds random number generator. Poor seeding enables prediction of 'random' values used in security contexts.
Binary parses formatted input. Buffer overflow risk if input size not bounded; format string bugs possible if user input reaches format string.
Binary outputs formatted data. If format string derives from user input, format string vulnerability enables memory disclosure/overwrite.
Binary formats strings into buffers. Classic buffer overflow risk if buffer size not validated; prefer snprintf().
Binary copies strings without bounds checking. Guaranteed overflow if source exceeds destination size; use strncpy() or strlcpy().
Binary copies strings with bounds. Safer than strcpy() but null termination issues possible; verify dest is always null-terminated.
Binary copies memory regions. Buffer overflow risk if count exceeds destination bounds; verify sizes carefully.
Binary moves overlapping memory regions. Similar overflow risk as memcpy() but handles overlaps safely.
Binary fills memory with pattern. Often used to clear sensitive data; verify it isn't optimized away by compiler for security purposes.
Binary allocates heap memory. Heap corruption vulnerabilities possible if size calculation overflows or free() is misused.
Binary allocates zeroed heap memory. Same heap corruption risks as malloc(); zero-initialization helps prevent information leakage.
Binary resizes heap allocation. Size parameter validation critical; integer overflow in size calculation could lead to undersized allocations.
Binary frees heap memory. Double-free, use-after-free, and heap corruption vulnerabilities possible; verify pointer validity.
Binary executes a program using an argument vector. Review the executable path, argument sources, and whether elevated privileges are dropped first.
Executes a program while searching PATH and accepting an explicit environment. Review PATH and environment sanitization when invoked with elevated privileges.
Executes a program by searching PATH. A writable or attacker-influenced PATH can cause unintended executable selection.
Creates a process and executes a program. Review executable selection, inherited file descriptors, environment, and privilege transitions.
Creates a process by searching PATH. Review PATH control and privilege handling.
Potential command-pipe use. Confirm whether shell commands incorporate untrusted input; the string alone does not prove a vulnerability.
References Bash. Determine whether it can be invoked with elevated privileges and whether privilege-dropping behavior is enforced.
References Dash shell. Investigate why a shell is used and whether arguments or environment are attacker-controlled.
References Zsh shell. Investigate shell invocation and privilege transitions.
Command string passed to a shell. If the command includes untrusted data, command injection may be possible.
Command string passed to Bash. Review input handling and execution privileges.
References executable search path. Check for relative, empty, or user-writable directories and environment sanitization.
References shell field-splitting configuration. Risk depends on whether it is used in shell execution or environment handling.
References environment configuration. Determine whether environment values can affect shell startup or privileged execution.
Bash may use this variable to select a startup file in noninteractive contexts. Review whether it is honored in a privileged execution path.
Python module search path may allow loading attacker-controlled modules if inherited by a privileged process.
Perl library search path can influence module loading. Review environment sanitization in privileged execution.
Ruby library search path can influence code loading. Review environment sanitization in privileged execution.
References the glibc character-conversion module path. Historically relevant to privilege escalation when unsafe environment values are honored; verify platform and mitigations.
References a name-service module path. Determine whether attacker-controlled modules could be loaded in a privileged process.
Dynamic-linker auditing environment variable. Verify privileged execution does not honor unsafe loader environment settings.
Dynamic-linker debugging variable. Usually diagnostic, but check whether sensitive loader output or environment handling matters.
Temporary-file creation is referenced. Check for predictable names, unsafe permissions, and whether creation is atomic.
Secure temporary-file creation primitive. Verify correct use, permissions, and cleanup.
Temporary-directory creation primitive. Verify permissions, path handling, and cleanup.
Legacy temporary-name function can be race-prone. Prefer secure creation APIs such as mkstemp.
Legacy temporary-name function can introduce race conditions because it returns a name without securely creating the file.
Opens a file or device. Review flags, permissions, path validation, and symlink handling; this common symbol alone is not a finding.
Opens a path relative to a directory descriptor. Review use of directory descriptors and flags such as O_NOFOLLOW where appropriate.
Uses Linux openat2 path-resolution controls. Verify restrictive resolution flags are applied when security boundaries matter.
References a flag that can prevent following a final symlink. Confirm it is applied to the relevant open operation; presence alone does not guarantee safety.
Creates files. Review requested permissions, umask, symlink behavior, and directory ownership.
Exclusive file creation flag. Check that it is paired appropriately with O_CREAT and used on a trustworthy filesystem.
Opens a stream by pathname. Review path control, permissions, and symlink/race handling.
Reopens a stream. Review target paths and effects on standard input/output/error in privileged code.
Wraps an existing file descriptor in a stream. Review descriptor provenance and access mode.
Reads from a file descriptor. Check return values, length bounds, and whether untrusted input is validated.
Writes to a file descriptor. Review destination descriptor, permissions, partial writes, and sensitive-file exposure.
Reads data into a buffer. Verify size/count calculations and handling of short reads.
Writes buffered data. Verify length calculations and whether sensitive data can be written to unintended destinations.
Unsafe C input function with no bounds checking. If present as an imported or reachable function, investigate immediately; modern toolchains may remove it.
Concatenates strings without destination-size checking. Review destination capacity and all input lengths.
Bounded string concatenation can still be misused if the bound is not the remaining destination capacity or termination is mishandled.
Formats data into a buffer without a size limit. Prefer vsnprintf and verify format strings are trusted.
Size-bounded formatting function. Verify return-value handling and ensure truncation does not create security issues.
Size-bounded formatted output. Verify buffer size and return-value handling.
Tokenizes strings in place. Review parsing assumptions and shared-state behavior when handling untrusted input.
Duplicates a string. Check allocation failure handling and the trustworthiness/size of the input.
Duplicates a bounded string. Check size limits and allocation failure handling.
Reads socket options. Usually benign; review network trust boundaries and error handling.
Changes socket options. Determine whether options affect security, binding, packet handling, or access controls.
Sends data on a socket. Review what data is transmitted and whether the peer is trusted.
Receives data from a socket. Validate lengths, framing, and all data before use.
Resolves host/service information. Review whether attacker-controlled names or service values influence privileged network activity.
Legacy hostname resolution API. Review input validation, resolver behavior, and error handling.
Password-hashing API reference. Verify algorithm choice, salt handling, and correct comparison/storage behavior.
Reentrant password-hashing API. Verify algorithm selection and safe handling of password material.
Looks up shadow-password records. Confirm access is intentional and password hashes are not exposed to untrusted users.
Starts a PAM authentication transaction. Review PAM configuration, service name, and error handling.
Performs PAM authentication. Verify failures are handled securely and authentication cannot be bypassed.
Sets PAM credentials. Review credential establishment and cleanup across success/failure paths.
Opens a PAM session. Review session setup, logging, and cleanup.
Generic authentication-related symbol/string. Investigate surrounding code; this marker alone does not establish an authentication flaw.
Authorization-related text. Review checks at sensitive operations; a string match alone is not proof of a defect.
References sudoers policy. Determine whether the program reads or modifies policy and whether paths/permissions are secure.
References SSH authorized_keys. Review whether the program can modify SSH access controls or write attacker-controlled keys.
References SSH host-key records. Review trust decisions and whether host-key checking is bypassed.
References SSH daemon configuration. Review any privileged write path for authorization and atomic safe updates.
References the system-wide dynamic-loader preload file. Any reachable privileged write path warrants immediate investigation.
References dynamic-loader configuration. Review whether privileged code can alter library search configuration.
References a cron configuration directory. Review whether untrusted users can influence files placed there.
References daily cron jobs. Determine whether the binary can write executable content into privileged scheduled-task locations.
References hourly cron jobs. Determine whether privileged scheduled tasks can be modified.
References system-wide systemd unit files. Review whether the program can create or modify privileged service definitions.
Shell command execution API reference. If this appears in a binary, inspect the call path and command construction; a string match alone does not prove exploitability.
References Linux capabilities. Inspect actual file/process capability assignments and whether the granted set is minimal.
References a broad Linux capability with extensive system-level authority. Verify whether it is granted or merely mentioned.
References the capability to manipulate user IDs. Verify actual capability assignments and privilege-transition logic.
References the capability to manipulate group IDs. Verify actual capability assignments and privilege-transition logic.
References bypassing discretionary file permission checks. Verify whether it is granted and constrained.
References bypassing file read/search permission checks. Verify whether it is granted and constrained.
References raw/packet socket capability. Determine whether the binary actually receives it and whether network access is necessary.
References syscall filtering. Review whether a restrictive filter is installed before processing untrusted input.
References libseccomp filter setup. Verify the filter is loaded successfully and denies the intended syscalls.
References Linux no_new_privs behavior. Confirm it is set at the appropriate point if relied upon as a security boundary.
References prctl option to prevent gaining new privileges through exec. Verify successful application and scope.
References seccomp setup through prctl. Verify the selected mode/filter and error handling.
Changes real, effective, and saved user IDs. Review ordering, return-value checks, and whether all saved privileges are dropped.
Changes real, effective, and saved group IDs. Review ordering and whether all saved privileges are dropped.
Changes effective user ID. Verify whether saved IDs allow privileges to be regained and whether failures are handled.
Changes effective group ID. Verify whether group privileges are dropped completely and failures are handled.
Changes filesystem user ID. Review filesystem permission semantics and privilege transition logic.
Changes filesystem group ID. Review filesystem permission semantics and privilege transition logic.
Generic capability-related marker. Verify actual process/file capability state rather than relying on string presence.
References audit logging. Verify security-relevant failures and privilege transitions are logged without leaking secrets.
Writes system log messages. Review format-string use and whether attacker-controlled content can forge or corrupt log entries.
Initializes syslog. Review identity/tag choices and whether sensitive data is logged.
Sets default file-creation permissions. Check that restrictive values are set before creating sensitive files.
Renames paths relative to directory descriptors. Review directory trust, race handling, and atomic update assumptions.
Removes a path relative to a directory descriptor. Review path validation and directory permissions.
Reads metadata from an open descriptor. Prefer descriptor-based checks when avoiding pathname races; verify checks apply to the descriptor later used.
Checks access to a path relative to a directory descriptor. Review TOCTOU exposure and whether the result is followed by a separate path operation.
Canonical path resolution call marker. Ensure the result is checked against an intended directory and not used as the sole defense against races.
References launching systemd transient units. Determine whether untrusted users can influence unit commands or properties.
References Docker tooling. If invoked with elevated privileges or access to the Docker socket, review whether it grants host-level control.
References Podman tooling. Review privileged mode, mounted host paths, and whether user-controlled arguments affect execution.
References mount namespace behavior. Verify namespace creation and mount propagation provide the intended isolation.
Creates namespaces. Review namespace flags and privileged operations performed inside them.
Joins an existing namespace. Verify target namespace descriptors are trusted and access is authorized.
Interacts with the kernel key-retention service. Review key permissions, namespace, and sensitive key material handling.
Requests a kernel key. Review key descriptions, request policy, and exposure of returned key material.
References reboot functionality. Confirm privileged reboot operations are authorized and not triggerable by untrusted input.
Changes I/O privilege level on supported architectures. If reachable, investigate closely because it can grant broad hardware access.
Changes process I/O port permissions. Verify privileged access is necessary and tightly constrained.
References loading a new kernel for kexec. Review privilege requirements and whether untrusted data can influence the image.
Loads a kernel module. Verify authorization and integrity of module paths/content.
Loads a kernel module from a file descriptor. Verify authorization and integrity of module content.
Removes a kernel module. Verify authorization and whether service/security impact is controlled.
References the BPF syscall. Review program type, verifier constraints, kernel version, and privilege checks.
Opens performance monitoring events. Review access controls and potential information exposure.
References user-account creation. Determine whether account creation is intended and input/authorization checks are enforced.
References modifying user accounts. Review group, shell, home-directory, and privilege changes.
References group creation. Review authorization and whether privileged group membership can be manipulated.
References bulk password changes. Verify input source, authorization, and protection of password data.
References sudoers editing utility. Review how it is invoked and whether arbitrary files or editor commands can be selected.
Editor-selection environment variable. If a privileged program launches an editor using this value, review command execution and environment sanitization.
Pager-selection environment variable. Some pagers support shell escapes; review privileged invocation and environment handling.
Less preprocessor environment variable. Review whether a privileged process invokes less or honors this variable.
Manual-page search path. Review only if it affects privileged file selection or subprocess execution.
Possible shell field-separator assignment. Inspect surrounding context; this substring can occur harmlessly.
References filesystem debugging tools that may permit low-level filesystem access. Determine whether privileged execution exposes raw device modification.
References a network scanning tool. Review privileged invocation, script execution features, and user-controlled arguments.
References BusyBox multi-call utilities. Determine which applet is invoked and whether command selection or paths are user-controlled.
References find command execution patterns. If used by privileged code, inspect command construction and directory/input trust.
References archive processing. Review extraction paths, symlink handling, and any privileged file writes.
References file synchronization. Review remote-shell invocation, destination paths, and privileged file permissions.
References secure-copy functionality. Review paths, host selection, and whether user-controlled arguments reach a privileged subprocess.
References HTTP transfer functionality. Review downloaded content integrity and whether privileged code executes or trusts remote data.
References download functionality. Review destination paths, TLS verification, and whether downloaded content is later executed.
References PAM configuration. Review any privileged write path and the effect on authentication policy.
References security configuration files. Determine whether the binary reads or modifies policy files and whether paths are trusted.
References host-name mapping configuration. Review privileged modifications and whether name resolution decisions can be manipulated.
References DNS resolver configuration. Review privileged modifications and resulting name-resolution trust.
References system-wide shell startup configuration. Review any privileged write path that could affect future shell sessions.
References system-wide environment configuration. Review privileged write access and variables that affect executable/module lookup.
References the dynamic-linker cache. Usually system-managed; investigate if privileged code writes or replaces it.
Uses the kernel random source. Verify errors are handled and enough entropy is obtained for security-sensitive values.
OpenSSL cryptographic random API. Verify return values are checked and failures do not fall back to predictable randomness.
References OpenSSL encryption setup. Review algorithm/mode selection, key/nonce handling, and authentication of ciphertext.
Configures TLS certificate verification. Check that verification is enabled and callbacks do not accept invalid certificates.
libcurl TLS peer-verification option. Ensure verification is enabled for connections where server identity matters.
libcurl hostname-verification option. Ensure hostname verification is enabled for authenticated TLS connections.
Converts error codes to text. Usually benign; avoid exposing sensitive internals in user-facing errors.
Assertion marker. Confirm security-critical checks are not implemented only as assertions that may be disabled.
Often indicates compiler stack-protector support. Positive hardening signal, but not proof that all unsafe paths are protected.
Often indicates fortified libc checks. Positive hardening signal, but does not establish overall binary safety.
Hardening marker. Verify actual ELF properties with tools such as checksec/readelf; string presence alone is not proof.
ELF stack metadata marker. Verify actual stack permissions in program headers rather than relying on string output.
References glibc symbol-version metadata. Useful for compatibility triage, not itself a vulnerability indicator.
